Dramatize

DRAM-uh-tyze · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To dramatize to exaggerate the importance or emotional impact of something.

The tabloid tends to dramatize even the most routine city council votes.

Worked Example

He dramatized a minor scheduling mix-up until it sounded like a full-blown crisis.

The mix-up itself was small and ordinary -- it was his retelling that inflated it into something far bigger, which is exactly dramatize.

How Dramatize Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

exaggerate

exaggerate: represent something as larger or more important than it is

sensationalize

sensationalize: present information in a way designed to trigger strong reactions

Antonyms

downplay

downplay: make something seem less important than it is

How Strong Is It? — emphasize → dramatize → sensationalize

emphasize vs. dramatize

emphasize vs. dramatize: Emphasizing something highlights its real importance; dramatizing it inflates that importance beyond what's actually there.

sensationalize vs. dramatize

sensationalize vs. dramatize: Dramatize can apply to any exaggeration, large or small; sensationalize specifically means presenting something in a shocking or scandalous way to trigger a reaction.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dramat

Root — dramat: a play, action (from Greek drama, whose stem is dramat-)

Suffix — -ize

Suffix — -ize: to make or cause to become (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Dramatize combines dramat ('a play, an action' -- the stem of Greek drama) with -ize ('to make') -- literally 'to turn into a drama,' treating an ordinary event as though it were a theatrical performance.

Use the root in a new word: drama

Use the root in a new word: drama: The root word drama itself comes from Greek dran, 'to do or act,' the same idea behind any staged performance.
